title: Before the Storm
subtitle: The plans, forces and criminal orders behind the opening assault
author: Robert M. Dobo
summary: Germany assembled an offensive intended to destroy the Soviet armies near the frontier. Its preparations joined operational confidence to an aggressive political project and an underestimate of the Soviet capacity to continue the war.
body:
An invasion assembled in the dark

On the evening of 21 June 1941, German formations stood ready to turn months of preparation into an invasion. Engineers and supply columns supported an offensive whose first tasks had been assigned; Soviet forces opposite them were still moving from military-district routines towards wartime deployment. The German situation sheet for that evening, preserved in an atlas compiled in 1942, records the disposition from the invader’s perspective. Behind its ordered symbols lay the question that would govern the first battles: which formations could receive instructions, move and fight together when the attack began? [1] German commanders hoped to reproduce the operational successes of 1939 and 1940 across a much greater territory. Their confidence rested partly on methods that had already worked, and partly on a serious underestimate of the Soviet state’s capacity to replace lost armies. Simultaneously, the regime had prepared a war in which military conquest, political destruction, racial persecution and economic exploitation would reinforce one another. The central contradiction was already present before a shot was fired: Germany was preparing a campaign whose political ambitions were almost unlimited while relying on military arrangements that required a rapid decision. [2] The frontier deployment concentrated both sides around a few operational problems. North of the Pripet Marshes, the German armies could converge on the Soviet forces projecting west around Białystok, then threaten the crossings leading into the interior. South of the marshes, an advance into Ukraine would encounter a different distribution of Soviet forces and a wider southern flank. The marshes restricted cooperation between those theatres. Destroying the forward armies therefore required several related operations whose results could not be assumed to arrive together. German confidence in a quick decision rested on solving those separate problems before Soviet reserves could establish another front. [3] For the inhabitants of the borderlands, even the word “frontier” concealed a recent history of violence. The Soviet Union had invaded eastern Poland in 1939 and forcibly annexed the occupied territory; it occupied and annexed Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia in 1940. Military control and Soviet annexation claims did not make the dispossession of these states an uncontested settlement. The earlier invasion and partition of Poland are examined in Ostkrieg’s Poland studies. Here its immediate significance is that millions of people were about to encounter another invading power, carrying its own prescriptions for who could live, who should work and who should disappear. [2]

From cooperation to a war of conquest

The German–Soviet arrangements of 1939 had made the partition of Poland possible and helped both dictatorships pursue their immediate objectives. They had not reconciled Hitler to the continued existence of the Soviet Union. After the defeat of France, Germany’s inability to bring Britain to terms sharpened his search for a decisive continental solution. Destroying the Soviet state promised, in his calculation, to remove a potential British partner, secure resources and open the east to German domination. Strategic calculation and ideological purpose therefore converged; one did not merely provide a respectable cover for the other. The German planning record places the development of this offensive in 1940, well before the immediate border alarms of June 1941. [3] That chronology matters to the later German claim of a preventive war. Soviet military thinking included offensive operations, and Soviet deployments were not those of a government indifferent to the possibility of war. Neither fact establishes that Germany’s attack was an emergency response to an imminent Soviet invasion. Hitler’s directive of 18 December 1940 instructed the armed forces to prepare to defeat the Soviet Union while the war against Britain continued. It also required subordinate orders to disguise those preparations as precautions against a possible change in Soviet behaviour. The document’s internal distinction between purpose and explanation is unusually revealing: the attack was being prepared; its concealment would invoke a hypothetical Soviet threat. [4] There was no single moment when all cooperation stopped and all hostility began. Trade, diplomacy and operational preparation could proceed simultaneously. Stalin sought to postpone a confrontation while improving the Soviet military position; Hitler could accept economic deliveries while assembling the force intended to destroy the delivering state. Interpreting the continued relationship as evidence of mutual confidence misses the coercive and instrumental character of the arrangement. It also exaggerates Stalin’s freedom to control its ending: avoiding an incident could reduce one pretext for war, but it could not cancel an invasion already chosen for broader reasons. [3] [2] Soviet expansion in 1939–40 altered this relationship between geography and readiness. The new frontier lay farther west, increasing the distance between an invading army and major interior centres, but the additional territory required garrisons, defensive construction and changes to communications and depots. Strategic depth—the space available to absorb an attack and organize further resistance—became useful only through the ability to employ it. Forward deployment could instead expose formations to enclosure before they withdrew. The Białystok salient was particularly vulnerable because its westward projection lay between German concentration areas, allowing threats to develop along both flanks of the Soviet position. [2]

What Directive 21 actually required

The first objective in Directive 21 was the destruction of the main Soviet forces in the western part of the country. German armoured thrusts were to prevent organized armies from retreating into the interior. Territorial advance mattered because it could produce that destruction and deprive surviving forces of bases; it was not supposed to substitute indefinitely for a decisive military result. The directive’s ultimate Volga–Archangel line expressed the intended scale of domination. From that barrier, the Luftwaffe was to suppress any remaining Soviet industrial power in the Urals. This was a program for destroying the state’s ability to resist, extending far beyond the frontier battles on which its feasibility depended. [4] The planning process also contained unresolved questions about priorities after the initial battles. Moscow was the central railway and political objective favoured by much of the army leadership. Hitler attached enormous importance to Leningrad, the Baltic region and the resources of Ukraine. The scheme north of the Pripet Marshes contemplated defeating the Soviet forces in Belarus and facilitating the destruction of those in the Baltic region before completing later advances. To reduce this to three independent races for three cities is to erase the intended interaction between the army groups and the disputes over what should happen once the frontier armies were beaten. [3] Directive 21 required preparations needing a long lead time to be completed by 15 May 1941. It did not fix that morning as the invasion date. The distinction matters when assessing the effect of the Balkan campaign and subsequent concentration problems: a readiness requirement cannot supply an exact measure of time lost on the road to Moscow. The directive committed Germany to a quick campaign, but whether that campaign could succeed depended on destroying Soviet military power, not simply on starting with more days of summer available. [4]

Reading the order

A preparation date is not a city deadline

The directive’s 15 May requirement concerned readiness for the operation. It does not establish that Minsk, Smolensk or Moscow had to fall on a particular day in June or July. Later studies compare events with specific orders where those exist, and with operational objectives where they do not. This prevents an attractive but misleading calendar of invented German deadlines. [4]

Poland and France had demonstrated the destructive power of penetration and encirclement. They had not demonstrated that the same methods would exhaust the Soviet Union’s ability to raise armies. That required a different judgment, embracing mobilization, industry, transport and political cohesion. German planners moved too readily from confidence in their own operational methods to confidence that the enemy could not recover from them. Racial contempt reinforced the underestimate. The plan’s greatest uncertainty was therefore concealed inside its central expectation: the destruction of the armies near the frontier was supposed to settle the much larger question of the Soviet state’s survival. [2]

Three army groups and four mobile striking forces

Army Group North, commanded by Wilhelm Ritter von Leeb, assembled in East Prussia. Georg von Küchler’s 18th Army and Ernst Busch’s 16th Army supplied the principal infantry formations, while Erich Hoepner’s 4th Panzer Group provided the mobile striking force. Their immediate theatre was Lithuania and Latvia, with crossings of the Western Dvina—Daugava in Latvia—essential to the continuation toward Pskov and Leningrad. The infantry and mobile forces had related but different jobs: a leading formation might secure a bridge while the following armies defeated bypassed resistance, widened the corridor and protected the route over which its supplies would have to pass. [2] [3] Army Group Centre, under Fedor von Bock, possessed the concentration most capable of producing a deep double envelopment. Hermann Hoth’s 3rd Panzer Group would strike from the northern side of the Białystok salient; Heinz Guderian’s 2nd Panzer Group would operate from the south, across the Bug in the Brest sector. Adolf Strauss’s 9th Army and Günther von Kluge’s 4th Army would attack between and behind them. Minsk lay beyond the salient, on the route toward the Berezina, the upper Dnieper and Smolensk. The two armoured groups gave Bock a capacity that neither neighbouring army group possessed in the same form: he could drive two major mobile arms around a concentration of Soviet forces rather than ask one arm to create the entire encirclement. [3] Gerd von Rundstedt’s Army Group South faced a different problem. Ewald von Kleist’s 1st Panzer Group, Walter von Reichenau’s 6th Army and Carl-Heinrich von Stülpnagel’s 17th Army would attack into western Ukraine. Farther south, Eugen Ritter von Schobert’s 11th Army and Romanian forces would operate from Romania. The northern striking force had to negotiate rivers, roads and Soviet concentrations while maintaining contact with infantry and protecting an exposed flank toward the Pripet region. The southern wing was initially assigned a more restricted role; a large offensive from the Prut would begin only in July. Treating the whole army group as if it crossed one starting line and advanced at one speed conceals those differences. [3] The German air forces were organized to support this operational design. Luftflotten 1, 2 and 4 supported the northern, central and southern sectors respectively, while retaining their own command arrangements. Their opening tasks included attacks on Soviet aviation and communications as well as direct support for the ground advance. Air superiority could isolate formations, disrupt a counterattack and make daylight movement exceptionally dangerous. It could not occupy a railway junction, repair a bridge or deliver all the fuel required by a panzer group. The partnership between aircraft and mobile ground forces was powerful precisely because their functions were complementary, not interchangeable. [2]

An army in the middle of becoming another army

Opposite these concentrations stood the western Soviet military districts. On the Baltic approaches, Fyodor Kuznetsov commanded the Baltic Special Military District, which would become the Northwestern Front. Dmitry Pavlov commanded the Western Special Military District, the basis of the Western Front. Mikhail Kirponos’s Kiev Special Military District would become the Southwestern Front. Markian Popov’s Leningrad district covered the northern approaches, while the southern command arrangements were being reorganized around forces in the Odessa district and a new Southern Front headquarters. A “front” in Soviet usage was a large operational command, broadly comparable to a German army group, rather than simply the line where soldiers were fighting. [2] The Soviet forces were substantial, but their organization was undergoing rapid expansion and repeated reconstruction. Mechanized corps were being created on a scale that outstripped the immediate supply of trained personnel, transport, maintenance facilities and communications equipment. The establishment of a headquarters and the assignment of tanks did not instantly create a force capable of moving, fuelling and fighting together. Jacob Kipp’s study of the covering forces is useful here because it distinguishes the intended role of the forward armies from the incomplete arrangements through which they had to perform it. They were supposed to protect mobilization and concentration while responding to an attack; in practice, German operations would begin disrupting those very processes before they were completed. [5] The T-34 and KV illustrate why equipment quality and formation readiness must be examined together. Armour and armament could give their crews a substantial advantage in a particular encounter, as the first week would demonstrate. Employing that advantage across a battle required trained personnel, suitable ammunition, fuel, recovery vehicles and timely information about friendly and enemy forces. A tank immobilized through mechanical failure or separated from its supporting arms could cease to influence the operation while remaining physically intact. Aggregate inventories combine vehicles in different conditions and locations; they cannot establish how many a commander could bring into action at a specified crossing. The later reputation of these weapons should therefore guide questions about their use, rather than determine the answer in advance. [2] The same caution applies to the effects of Stalin’s purges. The removal, imprisonment and killing of officers damaged the armed forces and encouraged a climate in which an incorrect judgment could become a political charge. But “the purges” cannot explain every broken radio, unfinished deployment or failed movement order. Expansion itself created a shortage of experienced officers; new organizations required new skills; recent reforms had not finished working through the army. These causes interacted. A rapidly promoted commander attempting to master an unfamiliar formation was doing so inside a political system that punished perceived disloyalty and made the reporting of unwelcome information dangerous. [2]

Warnings without an adequate response

The Soviet government did not lack warnings that Germany might attack. The difficulty lay in judging their reliability, their timing and their relationship to German deception and British interests. Stalin believed that Britain had an obvious incentive to bring Germany and the Soviet Union into conflict. He also understood that Germany faced the risks of fighting while Britain remained undefeated. Those considerations helped him discount information that should have carried greater weight. Explaining his reasoning does not make the outcome a blameless misunderstanding: authority was concentrated in a leader whose assumptions could restrict the response to accumulating evidence. [2] Soviet preparations nevertheless varied across services, districts and formations. Movement, reserve call-ups and local precautions indicate that the military apparatus was responding, although its measures did not produce a uniform state of readiness. Dispersal could protect equipment from air attack while making immediate concentration harder; moving a reserve could improve its prospective position while leaving it vulnerable in transit. Readiness should consequently be understood as a relationship among several conditions, rather than as a single order issued or withheld. The question for each formation is which measures had been completed, how they affected its assigned role and whether it retained the communications needed to coordinate action once fighting began. [2] The late-night directive associated with 21–22 June captured the tension. It warned of a possible attack, called for combat readiness and measures including the dispersal and concealment of aircraft, but also insisted that forces avoid provocations. Its transmission came too late to give all formations a common period in which to prepare. Commanders had to interpret urgent instructions through communications networks that were about to come under attack. A message received at an army or district headquarters was not simultaneously understood by every regiment, airfield and frontier post. [2]

A command distinction

Stalin was powerful before he held every wartime title

On the eve of invasion, Semyon Timoshenko was defence commissar and Georgy Zhukov chief of the General Staff. Stalin’s political authority was decisive, but the wartime Stavka had not yet been established. It would be created on 23 June with Timoshenko as chairman. Calling Stalin “supreme commander” in every formal sense on 21 June projects later appointments backwards. [6]

For commanders near the frontier, the late warning created an immediate dilemma. They had to prepare for an attack while avoiding actions Moscow might interpret as provocation. Preparations also depended on communications, transport and supplies that a warning could not create. The opening assault would force an abrupt change from restraint to counterattack, before many headquarters had established what remained of their formations. This was a failure in the relationship between political authority and military information. It exposed soldiers to incompatible demands at the moment when the ability to act together mattered most.

The coalition and the supply problem

Finland and Romania entered German planning for different reasons and under different arrangements. Finland sought to reverse losses imposed after the Winter War and increasingly cooperated militarily with Germany; Romania sought the recovery of Bessarabia and northern Bukovina, taken by the Soviet Union in 1940. Directive 21 anticipated the participation of both, but their forces were not simply additional German divisions. National command structures, territorial objectives and political calculations remained important. German operations from Finnish territory and the presence of German formations in Romania made cooperation materially significant before every formal declaration or major ground offensive had occurred. [4] The northern theatre in particular demands a separate clock. Operations from northern Finland toward Murmansk and the railway serving it were not identical to Army Group North’s advance from East Prussia. Distance, limited roads and difficult terrain constrained what could be accomplished there. The Soviet air attacks on Finland on 25 June and the Finnish government’s response would become important public markers of the Continuation War, but they should not erase the military cooperation already established. Conversely, Finland’s participation should not be described by simply transplanting the timing of German attacks in Lithuania onto the Karelian front. [3] Behind every sector lay the question of supply. German armies depended on railways for the large-scale movement of fuel, ammunition, food and replacements. Moving into the Soviet system required more than changing track gauge: bridges, locomotives, signalling, stations and damaged facilities affected the amount that could actually be delivered. Trucks extended the connection between railheads and fighting formations, but longer journeys consumed more fuel and vehicle life. Seizing a bridge intact was therefore valuable twice over, both for the immediate advance and for the maintenance of forces beyond it. [3] The popular picture of an entirely motorized German army is particularly misleading in this setting. The armoured and motorized formations formed a striking minority inside an army whose infantry usually marched and whose transport included enormous numbers of horses. Ziemke and Bauer give approximately 600,000 motor vehicles and 625,000 horses for the initial Barbarossa force; the figures describe the mixed character of the whole undertaking, not a uniform allowance per division. A mobile spearhead could move far ahead while the men required to secure its flanks and reduce pockets were still approaching on foot. That separation would become one of the campaign’s recurring operational problems. [2]

The orders behind the front line

Before the invasion, German authorities had also altered the conditions under which soldiers were to treat civilians and prisoners. The decree of 13 May on military jurisdiction in the Barbarossa area empowered officers to shoot civilians suspected of hostile acts outside ordinary judicial proceedings. It also removed the normal obligation to prosecute German personnel for offences against civilians, except where military discipline or security required action. The decree supplied authority for violence before the army encountered the population. Keitel’s later examination at Nuremberg concerned a document he had signed, although his testimony defending his conduct requires its own scrutiny. The policy cannot be explained as an improvised response to resistance first encountered after the invasion. [7] The Commissar Order of 6 June went further by directing the separation and killing of captured Soviet military political commissars, officers responsible for political supervision and education. It expressly denied them the protection normally associated with prisoners of war. The order’s ideological language treated political office as a reason for execution, turning capture into an occasion for selection and murder. Its existence prevents a separation of Barbarossa into a supposedly conventional military campaign followed by an unrelated SS war. The army’s own preparations included instructions to murder particular captives; the next study examines evidence that these instructions were implemented from the invasion’s opening. [8]

The language of concealed preparation

An offensive presented as a precaution

Section IV of Directive 21 required subordinate orders to describe their measures as precautions against a possible change in Soviet conduct. It also restricted the number of officers informed and delayed briefing additional personnel. These provisions sit within a directive explicitly preparing an offensive. Their juxtaposition provides documentary evidence of concealment: the explanation to be circulated through the command system differed from the operation’s stated purpose.

[4]
Food policy made the connection between military supply and civilian destruction equally explicit. Economic directives dated 23 May proposed diverting agricultural surpluses from the Soviet south toward German requirements, cutting the northern forest zone and its industrial cities off from their usual supplies. The planners anticipated mass starvation or flight and rejected feeding the affected population if that competed with Germany’s war needs. Presented at Nuremberg as document EC-126, the directives reveal intended deprivation before the invasion, rather than a famine that authorities had merely failed to foresee. They do not establish deaths already caused on 21 June, or the exact later implementation in every district. They establish that feeding the occupying forces and exploiting the conquered economy were being planned through the deliberate abandonment of other people’s survival. [9] Germany had assembled forces capable of inflicting a major defeat at the frontier, while its planning remained dependent on assumptions about what such a defeat would do to the Soviet state. The Soviet leadership had failed to translate warnings and resources into a sufficiently coordinated response before the attack. These judgments concern different responsibilities: German preparations served an aggressive project of conquest, whereas Soviet errors increased the vulnerability of the army and population confronting it. The opening assault would put both systems into action and reveal the uneven relationship between the destruction of formations, the survival of resistance and the capacity to continue the war.

sourceMethod: Numbered citations identify the passages used. Soviet documents are accessed in published transcriptions, not as original archive files; their archival references are those printed by the editors. Orders establish intended actions, while reports preserve contemporary estimates and gaps. German operational histories are read with their dependence on German records and postwar testimony in mind. Perpetrator documents are distinguished from neutral counts, and later recollections from contemporary testimony. The 17 October 2026 editorial report distinguishes newly inspected passages from the documented source checks retained from 16 October; some publisher pages remain access-limited.
